newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE - Germans cling to little oasis in rural South Africa.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Germans cling to little oasis in rural South Africa.

text.p: Hidden in highland wheat fields and pine forests is an oasis of Germany that generations of South Africans have preserved.
Hermannsburg looks very much like hundreds of other farming hamlets that dot the landscape of central Europe.
Only a few palm trees, the locals' patchy accents and the small buildings of Zulu Hermannsburg up the road give the game away.
The butcher's leberwurst is excellent, families wish each other Guten Appetit, the affluent drive BMWs and Volkswagens and an Oompah band competition is held yearly.

"The place reminded me totally of home when I arrived," said vicar Hans-Ulrich Kruse, heading back to Germany after seven years at the brown stone Peter-Paul Church that dominates the remote hamlet in the province of KwaZulu-Natal.

His replacement was to be chosen by the parishioners from audio cassette auditions sent by hopefuls from the German headquarters of the Lutheran mission society. It founded the settlement 150 years ago in the wild frontier grassland.
Immigrants have come to South Africa for centuries and are still pouring in, most recently from other African countries.
But most head for cities and it is rare to find rural communities like Hermannsburg, with its one street of 14 homes, a church, a school and a shop, Boehling's Supply Store.
Scores more German families live out on nearby farms.
"We call ourselves the Springbok Germans," said Omi Kassier, 90.
"Through church and school we have kept our German culture strong," said Inge von Fintel, showing visitors around the Hermannsburg mission house-museum, built in 1855.
"We are confident we'll keep it going. Our children still speak German, although they are no longer quite as serious about it as we are."
In a country that preached racial separateness, it was easy for the close-knit community, one of the earliest German settlements in Africa, to stick to its own ways.

To themselves and other South Africans, they are still very Teutonic, despite the corrupting influence of English on their speech -- der Farmer and der Fridge instead of der Bauer and der Kuelschrank -- and of time and distance on their character.
Some visitors from Germany, however, find them trapped in a timewarp, fondly remembering a homeland many have never seen and which has changed vastly since their ancestors set sail.
"They have a perception of Germany that has got very little to do with the Germany I know," said Stephan Homberg from Hamelin, a trainee teacher at Hermannsburg German school.
"They need their German roots much more than people in Germany who, by the way, don't drink as much as the people here think we do."
Busloads of curious German tourists, a trickle of teachers and Lutheran evangelists from HQ in northern Germany's Lueneburg Heath keep links with the old country alive.

"The fresh input here from Germany has made people more open than Afrikaners," said Homberg, making a comparison with the creators of apartheid. The Afrikaners are descended from Dutch settlers and French and German arrivals they absorbed.
A cash grant from the German government enables temporary teachers to come over to Hermannsburg and keep language standards up to scratch, for the children at least.
The church school of some 200 pupils was one of South Africa's first to open its doors to all races in the 1980s.
It is one of a handful of German schools in South Africa and neighbouring Namibia, an ex-colony run briefly from Berlin, which still retains its German street names and beer gardens.
Hermannsburg's church also succumbed to racial segregation.
In the 1920s, long before apartheid, it went whites-only like most churches in the then British dominion. The Zulus were moved up the road to a separate, makeshift church.
The vicar and Mrs von Fintel said efforts were now being made to reunite the two congregations, whose church forebears were the first to translate the Bible into Zulu.

"Relations with blacks are more open today. We have tried to have more to do with them, but it's not easy," said von Fintel, whose family has lived here for generations and still enjoys hearty dinners of eisbein (pork knuckle) and sauerkraut.
"We have invited them for joint services but they have not asked us over very much," the wife of the museum curator added.
The graveyard has also stayed exclusive. No Zulu names are to be found amid the Boehlings, Luedemanns and Boehmers in the neat tree-lined plot beside the church.
